title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 7: Understanding China
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's December 21, 2008 Inquirer column on 'understanding China,' framed by President Arroyo's eight China visits in seven years (versus her predecessors' one apiece) and the country's rising importance
China's 'phenomenal economic boom' -- the world's 'best performing economy,' resilient against recession amid the global meltdown and pump-priming with a $586-billion stimulus

His travel impressions of an Olympics-transformed, 'space-age' Beijing and Shanghai -- the 'Bird's Nest,' the 'Egg' and the 'Water Cube' designed on yin and yang, the CCTV towers, and skyscrapers said to outnumber New York's

China as a restored 'global super power' -- Olympic champion, third nation to orbit a citizen, runner of the world's fastest trains -- that has 'healed the scars' of the Opium Wars and 'regained its national greatness' among the powers of the 21st century
sub_topics: The frame: Arroyo 'visited China at least eight times' in seven years (six in 2006-2008), against predecessors who 'went to China only once' -- Marcos (1975, who 'reestablished diplomatic relations'), Cory (1988), Ramos (1993) and Estrada (2000) -- a frequency CJP ties to 'the growing importance of China'
The economic boom: in 2007 the Philippines exported more to China than it imported, while China itself exported far more than it imported, 'making it the world's best performing economy'

Resilience: China's growth would slow to about 9 percent (then ~8 percent) amid the global meltdown, 'but unlike the other economic superpowers (United States, Europe, and Japan), it will not suffer recession,' and was spending '$586 billion to stimulate' activity via 'new infrastructure, homes, schools, and hospitals'

An Olympics-made metropolis: the Games 'transform[ed] Beijing into a bustling space-age metropolis,' the Aug. 8, 2008 opening being the deadline for 'newest wonders' -- the 'Bird's Nest' National Stadium, the 'Egg' National Theater, and the 'Water Cube' Aquatic Center

Yin and yang: these 'behemoths,' though cyber-age, were 'designed with traditional Chinese yin and yang' -- the square Water Cube denoting earth and femininity, the round red Bird's Nest heaven and masculinity -- modern equals of 'the Great Wall, the... Forbidden City, and the... Summer Palace'

Marvels and meals: he was 'dazzled' by the Capital airport, 'seven-star hotels,' malls and global cuisines, the gravity-defying CCTV towers, and Shanghai skyscrapers 'said to outnumber those in New York' -- and savored Peking duck at DaDong and dinners hosted by Xiao Yang, retired chief justice of China's Supreme People's Court, and Ambassador Sonia Brady

Global superpower: beyond economics, China is the 'overall Olympic champion,' the third nation 'which can orbit its citizens in space' (after Russia and the US), and runs 'the fastest trains in the world, the Maglev' (up to 501 kph) -- 'politically stable, economically dynamic, and technologically advanced'

Healed humiliation: modern China 'has regained its national greatness' and 'healed the scars of humiliation' from the Opium Wars and the 'unequal treaties' (dramatized in '55 Days in Peking'); its 1961 'National Humiliation Day' explains why 'foreign criticisms' trigger 'extreme restiveness' -- but it can now be proud of '5,000 years' of legacy and 'its secure place among the greatest global powers of the 21st century'

events: the 2008 Beijing Olympics; Arroyo's China visits; the global financial meltdown; the 'Shenzhou' space flight

stances.claim: China's frequent courtship by President Arroyo reflects 'the growing importance of China to our country and the rest of the world' -- by 2007 'the world's best performing economy,' resilient against the recession that struck the US, Europe and Japan.
stances.rhetorical_move: frequency-as-signal: reading state visits as a marker of China's rising weight

stances.claim: China marries the cyber-age with tradition -- its Olympic 'behemoths' designed on yin and yang -- and has restored its 'national greatness,' becoming a stable, dynamic, technologically advanced power.
stances.rhetorical_move: synthesis-portrait: pairing modern marvels with ancient symbolism

stances.claim: Modern China has 'healed the scars of humiliation' from the Opium Wars and unequal treaties -- its 'National Humiliation Day' explaining its sensitivity to criticism -- and now holds 'a secure place among the greatest global powers of the 21st century.'
stances.rhetorical_move: historical-framing: explaining the present through the arc from humiliation to greatness

notable_anecdotes: Eight visits to one: CJP contrasts Arroyo's eight China trips in seven years with predecessors who each went only once -- Marcos having 'reestablished diplomatic relations' in 1975.
Yin and yang in steel: he notes the Olympic 'Bird's Nest' and 'Water Cube' were designed on traditional yin and yang -- heaven and earth, masculine and feminine.
Maglev in minutes: he marvels that China's Maglev train, at up to 501 kph, covers the 30 km to Shanghai's airport in 'seven minutes and 20 seconds.'
Duck and a Chinese chief justice: he recalls Peking duck at DaDong and dinners hosted by Xiao Yang, retired chief justice of China's Supreme People's Court.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's December 21, 2008 Inquirer column, is an essay on 'understanding China,' framed by President Arroyo's eight China visits in seven years -- against predecessors who each 'went to China only once' (Marcos in 1975, who 'reestablished diplomatic relations,' Cory in 1988, Ramos in 1993, Estrada in 2000) -- which CJP ties to 'the growing importance of China.' He surveys its 'phenomenal economic boom': by 2007 'the world's best performing economy,' and, amid the global meltdown, set to slow to about 9 percent yet, 'unlike the other economic superpowers,' avoid recession while spending '$586 billion to stimulate' activity. Recounting his own travels, he describes an Olympics-transformed 'space-age' Beijing -- the 'Bird's Nest' National Stadium, the 'Egg' National Theater, and the 'Water Cube' designed on 'traditional Chinese yin and yang' (earth and heaven, feminine and masculine) -- alongside the gravity-defying CCTV towers and Shanghai skyscrapers 'said to outnumber those in New York,' plus Peking duck at DaDong and dinners hosted by Xiao Yang, retired chief justice of China's Supreme People's Court. Beyond economics, China is the 'overall Olympic champion,' the third nation able to 'orbit its citizens in space,' and runner of 'the fastest trains in the world, the Maglev' (501 kph). 'Politically stable, economically dynamic, and technologically advanced,' modern China 'has regained its national greatness' and 'healed the scars of humiliation' from the Opium Wars and the 'unequal treaties' -- its 1961 'National Humiliation Day' explaining its restiveness at criticism -- taking 'its secure place among the greatest global powers of the 21st century.'
